entry.title: Kristen Hendricks: Symmetries of Knots and Khovanov's Homology (TSVP Talk at OIST)

author.name: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)

media:group.media:title: Kristen Hendricks: Symmetries of Knots and Khovanov's Homology (TSVP Talk at OIST)
media:group.media:description:
Title: Symmetries of Knots and Khovanov's Homology
Speaker: Kristen Hendricks, Rutgers University
Abstract: A knot is an embedding of a circle into standard three-dimensional space. Knots are special objects in topology because they are very concrete and tractable, but they have deep connections to three- and four-dimensional geometry, which is generally much harder to visualize and understand. One aspect of knot theory that is currently enjoying a lot of attention is knots with symmetries, which is to say knots which are preserved by some reflection or rotation of three-dimensional space. Khovanov homology is an invariant of knots which was introduced around 2000. It has a deceptively simple construction, easy to describe on a blackboard, but encodes a wealth of geometric information. However, it turns out to be difficult to extract any good statements about knot symmetry from Khovanov homology in its original form. We discuss various ways one might upgrade such a theory geometrically to better understand its behavior in the presence of symmetry.
Profile: Kristen Hendricks is a professor at Rutgers University working in low-dimensional and symplectic topology. Most of her research is on equivariant versions of various Floer-theoretic invariants of knots and three-manifolds. She obtained her PhD from Columbia in 2013, after which she was a postdoc at UCLA and an assistant professor at Michigan State before moving to Rutgers in 2019.

entry.title: Sue-Hyun Lee: How the Brain Organizes and Reshapes Experience (TSVP Talk at OIST)

author.name: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)

media:group.media:title: Sue-Hyun Lee: How the Brain Organizes and Reshapes Experience (TSVP Talk at OIST)
media:group.media:description:
Title: How the Brain Organizes and Reshapes Experience
Speaker: Sue-Hyun Lee
Abstract: The brain does not simply represent and store information as it is received from the external world. In the first part of this talk, I will show how information from different sensory modalities can be represented in a common, supramodal format, and how complex social information can be organized along meaningful neural dimensions. In the second part, I will show that these representations are not stored in a fixed form, but continue to change during memory encoding, consolidation, and retrieval. Together, these findings highlight the flexible nature of neural representations that allows experience to be transformed into memory and used to guide behavior.
Profile: Dr. Lee is an Associate Professor in the Department of Psychology at Seoul National University. Her research focuses on how cognitive information is organized and dynamically reorganized in the human brain, with a particular emphasis on the neural mechanisms of memory. She received her B.S. in Physics from KAIST and Ph.D. in Neurobiology from Seoul National University. Following postdoctoral training at the NIMH/NIH, where she studied neural representations of perception, imagery, and working memory using fMRI, she joined the faculty at KAIST in 2015 and moved to Seoul National University in 2023.

entry.title: Hyoung Kim: Parallel and Convergent Processing of Value Information... (TSVP Talk at OIST)

author.name: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)

media:group.media:title: Hyoung Kim: Parallel and Convergent Processing of Value Information... (TSVP Talk at OIST)
media:group.media:description:
Title: Parallel and Convergent Processing of Value Information in the Primate Basal Ganglia
Speaker: Hyoung F. Kim
Abstract: Primates possess specialized neural circuits that support efficient value-guided behavior. Here, I focus on two organizational principles of the primate basal ganglia: parallel processing for cognitive flexibility and habitual stability, and convergent processing of value information across sensory modalities. Flexible and stable object values are processed in parallel along the rostral–caudal axis of the basal ganglia. Rostral circuits support flexible updating of object values, whereas caudal circuits maintain stable, long-term values that guide habitual behavior. Beyond this parallel organization, primates integrate value information across sensory modalities, including vision and fingertip touch. We show that striatal neurons encode tactile value and that visual and tactile value signals converge at the single-neuron level, providing an efficient substrate for value abstraction. Despite this convergence, population activity retains sensory modality information, while greater similarity of value representations across modalities is associated with better decision-making performance. Together, these findings reveal parallel specialization and multimodal convergence as complementary principles of value processing in the primate basal ganglia.
Profile: Hyoung F. Kim is an Associate Professor in the School of Biological Sciences at Seoul National University, where he leads the Cognitive Circuitry Laboratory. He studies the neural circuit mechanisms underlying value-based decision-making in primates, with a particular focus on the basal ganglia. He is particularly interested in how parallel neural circuits support cognitive flexibility and habitual stability, and how neuronal populations integrate sensory and value information for efficient decision-making. He received his undergraduate degree in Biotechnology from the College of Engineering at Yonsei University and his PhD from Seoul National University under the mentorship of Dr. Bong-Kiun Kaang, studying transcriptional mechanisms underlying long-term memory. He subsequently conducted postdoctoral research with Dr. Okihide Hikosaka at the National Institutes of Health, investigating the neural mechanisms of value process in primates.

entry.title: Understanding ADHD: From Childhood Support to Women's Experiences

author.name: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)

media:group.media:title: Understanding ADHD: From Childhood Support to Women's Experiences
media:group.media:description:
In this recorded seminar, two leading ADHD researchers share insights into ADHD across different stages of life. Professor Gail Tripp (OIST) discusses behavioral approaches to supporting children with ADHD, including practical strategies for everyday situations. Professor Annabeth Groenman (University of Amsterdam) explores ADHD in women and girls, highlighting how its characteristics and impact may change across the lifespan.
These two talks were presented as part of the public seminar Updates on Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), hosted by the OIST Children's Research Center.

media:group.media:title: Provost Lecture Series: Kenji Doya
media:group.media:description:
Speaker: Kenji Doya, Professor, Neural Computation Unit
Title: Reinforcement learning in the brain and robots
Abstract: Reinforcement learning is a theoretical framework for an active agent, either human, animal, robot, or software, to learn actions guided by reward signal evaluating its performance. Since the start or our Neural Computation Unit in 2004, revealing the brain’s mechanisms for reinforcement learning and developing more flexible reinforcement learning mechanisms for robots have been the major dual goals. In this lecture, I will present our works till today about how the basal ganglia evaluate the goodness of actions, how the network linking the cortex, the basal ganglia and the cerebellum can realize action planning by mental simulation, and how the serotonergic system balance short- and long-term evaluation. I will also introduce our ongoing works on how prediction and control can be realized in the cortical circuits, and how rewards can be evolved for survival, reproduction, and curiosity.
The Provost Lecture Series will provide an opportunity to celebrate milestones in the careers of OIST faculty members. It will recognize newly promoted professors and those who have received prestigious awards. It will highlight faculty achievements and create a space for retiring professors to talk about their research accomplishments and lessons learned over the course of their career. It is a way to celebrate OIST faculty, introduce them to the broader OIST community, acknowledge their research successes, share about their teaching and mentorship of students, and honor their service to the university.

entry.title: Developing machine learning tools to standardize the identification of microplastics

author.name: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)

media:group.media:title: Developing machine learning tools to standardize the identification of microplastics
media:group.media:description:
To address the growing problem of microplastics in the natural environment, Dr. Samantha Phan, a recipient of the Technology Pioneer Fellowship of the OIST Proof of Concept (POC) Program, has been developing a machine learning tool for spectral analysis. By creating a rich identification system for microplastics using thousands of collected samples, Dr. Phan is bringing her research and technical skills into the real world and applying them to the problem of microplastics pollution.
Having developed this machine learning tool, Dr. Phan hopes to reach more users interested in implementing this microplastics identification technology, ultimately better understanding the understanding of the extent of microplastic pollution across different industries and contributing to the standardization of microplastic indentification.
Speaker: Dr. Samantha Phan, pi-Conjugated Polymers Unit More information in English: https://www.oist.jp/innovation/poc/77-phan-0 More information in Japanese: https://www.oist.jp/ja/innovation/poc/77-phan-0

media:group.media:description:
Starting from just a sheet of paper, by folding, stacking, crumpling, tearing, we shall explore a rich variety of phenomena, from magic tricks and geometry through elasticity and the traditional Japanese art of origami to medical devices and ‘h-principle’. Much of the lecture consists of table-top demos, which you can later try with family and friends.
So, take a sheet of paper . . .
Tadashi Tokieda is a professor at Stanford. He grew up as a painter in Japan, became a classical philologist (not to be confused with philosopher) in France, worked a little as a plumber, earned a PhD in pure mathematics at Princeton, and has since been doing applied mathematics around the world. He is also active in outreach, especially via the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences and the YouTube channel Numberphile.

media:group.media:title: 時枝 正 - 数も式もない計算
media:group.media:description:
概要 人——プロの数学者も含めて——は「計算」というと数や式の操作を連想しがちです。おしなべて「数学」というと定義がはっきりした形式だ、と思い込みます。しかし人の知能は、形式の外、定義以前、数も式もない場で計算を始められるのがその本質なのです。それを手品でご説明しましょう。子どもにも楽しめ、立派な研究者にもふしぎな手品で。

entry.title: Rong Tong: Machine Learning Guided Discovery of Stereoselective Polymerization Catalysts (TSVP Talk)

author.name: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)

media:group.media:title: Rong Tong: Machine Learning Guided Discovery of Stereoselective Polymerization Catalysts (TSVP Talk)
media:group.media:description:
Title: Machine Learning Guided Discovery of Stereoselective Polymerization Catalysts
Speaker: Rong Tong, Virginia Tech
Abstract: Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is a leading biodegradable and biocompatible polymer with growing importance in the plastics industry. Stereoselective ring-opening polymerization of lactide provides access to stereoregular PLA with thermal and mechanical properties superior to those of atactic PLA. However, the discovery of highly stereoselective polymerization catalysts remains largely empirical, relying on extensive synthesis and experimental screening. To address this challenge, we developed an integrated computational–experimental framework for efficient and predictive catalyst discovery and optimization. We first established a Bayesian optimization workflow using a subset of literature data on stereoselective lactide ring-opening polymerization. Guided by this algorithm, we identified multiple new aluminum complexes exhibiting either isoselective or heteroselective polymerization behavior. We expanded this framework by incorporating in-loop analysis and global–local molecular descriptors, enabling the discovery of highly efficient enantioselective catalysts to produce stereocomplex PLA, which exhibits enhanced thermal and mechanical properties compared to other PLA stereoisomers.
Profile: Dr. Rong Tong received his Ph.D. degree in Materials Science and Engineering from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 2010, working on the synthesis and formulation of novel nanomedicines for targeted cancer therapy. He was a postdoctoral associate at both Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Langer lab) and Harvard Medical School (Kohane lab) during 2010 to 2015. He is currently an Associate Professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering at Virginia Tech. His research interests include polymer chemistry, nanomedicine, biomaterials and targeted cancer therapy. He is the recipient of Thieme Chemistry Journals Award (2020), Class of Influential Researcher of Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research (2017), Emerging Investigator of Biomaterials Science (2017), American Chemical Society AkzoNobel Award in polymer chemistry (2010), Racheff-Intel Graduate Student Research Award (2009), the Siteman Center for Cancer Nanotechnology Fellowship (2007).

entry.title: Amaury Micheli: Spontaneous quasiparticle creation in an analogue preheating experiment (TSVP Talk)

author.name: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)

media:group.media:title: Amaury Micheli: Spontaneous quasiparticle creation in an analogue preheating experiment (TSVP Talk)
media:group.media:description:
Title: Spontaneous quasiparticle creation in an analogue preheating experiment
Speaker: Amaury Micheli, RIKEN Center for Interdisciplinary Theoretical and Mathematical Sciences (iTHEMS)
Abstract: First, I will briefly outline the motivations and concepts that underpin the analogue gravity program. Next, I will provide a detailed description of a specific experiment designed to simulate various features of the cosmological reheating era. Finally, I will present our recent experimental results from this setup, where we demonstrated the parametric creation of quasiparticle pairs from the quantum vacuum, drawing an analogy with the preheating phase of reheating.
Profile: Amaury Micheli is a postdoctoral researcher at RIKEN iTHEMS in Wako, Japan. His research seeks evidence for the quantum nature of gravity by identifying and quantifying quantum correlations in settings where gravitational, or gravity-like, and quantum effects coexist; from the primordial inhomogeneities generated during inflation to laboratory analogues of curved spacetime. Amaury's work combines analytical field theory, numerical and semi-classical simulation, and close collaboration with experimental teams, including the observation of spontaneous pair creation in a cold-atom analogue of cosmological preheating. His research is strongly interdisciplinary, importing quantum-information tools into cosmology and testing high-energy vacuum amplification predictions in table-top experiments.

entry.title: Federico Toschi: The Physics of Flowing Human Crowds (TSVP Talk at OIST)

author.name: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST)

media:group.media:title: Federico Toschi: The Physics of Flowing Human Crowds (TSVP Talk at OIST)
media:group.media:description:
Title: The Physics of Flowing Human Crowds
Speaker: Federico Toschi, Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e).
Abstract: The dynamics of human crowds is a paramount example of active matter physics with outstanding societal relevance [1]. Understanding and predicting the dynamics of human crowds is key to our daily comfort and safety and efficiency when moving in crowded urban areas. On the basis of a vast collection of experimental recordings, of highly space- and time-accurate trajectories of single individuals in (dense) crowds, we discuss quantitative models capable of explaining and predicting, at a statistical level, the dynamics of human crowds in simple flow configurations [2]. In this talk, we will start by reviewing the basic phenomenology of human crowds, along with a discussion of the simple physics-based models formulated on the basis of Langevin equations and path integrals. Finally, we discuss the most generic phenomenology of human crowd flows and we present a model, based on the coupled dynamics of slow and fast variables, capable of quantitatively describing the behaviour of single individuals in a crowd under very general flow conditions. This model can be used as a framework to infer physics-based models from data.
Profile: Federico Toschi is a full professor in the Department of Applied Physics at Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e). His research focuses on emerging complexity in challenging multiscale problems at the crossroads of statistical physics, fluid mechanics, soft condensed matter, and biophysics. Federico’s research employs experimental, numerical, and theoretical methods and covers, among other topics, fluid-dynamics turbulence; Lagrangian turbulence; thermal convection; complex fluids; soft condensed matter; active matter; crowd dynamics; scientific computing; and Lattice Boltzmann methods. Several of Federico’s research topics are strongly interdisciplinary and involve pushing the boundaries of physics across different disciplines.
